patient.name: Daniel Okafor
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then Liver Intensive Care
patient.complaint: Three days of vomiting and right-sided abdominal pain, now drowsy and muddled
background: Took extra paracetamol and co-codamol for 3 days for a dental abscess
Drinks about 40 units of alcohol a week
Lives alone in Lewisham; sister brought him in

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with jaundice, confusion and an INR above 1.5, or 'Which is the most likely finding?' (asterixis). Causes asked: paracetamol, alcohol, viral, Budd-Chiari, acute fatty liver of pregnancy.

points: Daniel, 36, took **extra paracetamol** for 3 days for toothache.
Now vomiting, with pain under his right ribs.
His sister says he is **confused** and sleepy today.
Drinks about 40 units of alcohol a week.

steps.lead: Daniel's liver has lost its **synthetic, metabolic and detoxifying** work all at once. Paracetamol is the cause, alcohol the accomplice.

visual.title: Where Daniel's pain is
visual.caption: A tender, smooth liver edge in the RUQ: the swollen, necrotic liver stretching its capsule.

points: He is **jaundiced**, with a tender smooth liver edge.
Arms outstretched, wrists dorsiflexed: a coarse **flapping tremor**.
No spider naevi, no ascites, no splenomegaly.

steps.q: Which sign tells you Daniel is in liver failure, not just liver injury?
steps.r: **Asterixis** is hepatic encephalopathy, a cardinal feature of liver failure. Jaundice and hepatomegaly occur with any hepatitis.

steps.lead: Daniel has rapid deterioration, encephalopathy and (we will see) an INR above 1.5: **acute** liver failure, not chronic. No stigmata of cirrhosis.
Vomiting, RUQ pain, a tender liver edge and asterixis days after overdose: the **hepatic phase** of paracetamol toxicity.

steps.title: Acute vs chronic vs acute-on-chronic liver failure
head: Feature
Acute
Chronic (decompensated)
Acute-on-chronic

steps.lead: Daniel's story fits paracetamol. Other causes to keep in mind: **Budd-Chiari** (pain, ascites, hepatomegaly), **acute fatty liver of pregnancy**, and haemochromatosis.

steps.text: Do not call Daniel's confusion alcohol withdrawal or Wernicke's. Confusion plus **asterixis** plus a high INR in a jaundiced patient is **hepatic encephalopathy**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the INR (prothrombin time) defines acute liver failure, and a paracetamol level or viral serology finds the cause.

steps.title: Daniel's bloods on arrival
steps.text: Huge transaminases with a modest ALP and bilirubin rise; the **INR** shows the liver cannot make clotting factors.

steps.lead: Daniel's first-line panel: LFTs, **INR**, U&Es and glucose (he is hypoglycaemic), clotting, and an ultrasound of his liver.

visual.title: Daniel's INR
visual.label: Daniel 4.2
visual.caption: INR above 1.5 with encephalopathy defines acute liver failure.

steps.lead: Clinical picture plus LFTs and INR make the diagnosis; Daniel's **INR of 4.2** is the defining coagulopathy.

steps.q: What will identify the cause of Daniel's liver failure?
steps.r: **Paracetamol level** and **viral serology** find the cause. A staggered overdose can give a low level, so the history matters too.

steps.lead: Daniel's paracetamol level is detectable despite the last dose being 10 hours ago; hepatitis A, B, C and E serology are negative.

steps.title: Arterial blood gas
steps.text: A metabolic acidosis after paracetamol is a poor prognostic sign (King's College Criteria).

steps.lead: Daniel's encephalopathy is graded: drowsy with a flap is **grade II**, and grade worsens as he becomes more obtunded.

visual.title: Hepatic encephalopathy grade
visual.label: Daniel grade II
visual.caption: Asterixis appears at grades II–III; grade III/IV counts in King's criteria.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (NAC, lactulose, IV ceftriaxone for SBP) or 'next step' when King's College Criteria are met (urgent transplant referral).

steps.q: Daniel's overdose was staggered and he now has liver failure. What is the first treatment for the cause?
steps.r: **NAC** is given in any staggered overdose or established liver injury, whatever the level. Charcoal is only useful within an hour.

steps.lead: Daniel gets **IV NAC**, 10% dextrose for his glucose of 3.1, electrolyte correction and careful coagulopathy management, and is moved to **ICU**.
His grade II encephalopathy is treated with **lactulose**; mannitol would be needed if cerebral oedema developed, after checking his heart.

visual.title: Daniel's first 72 hours
visual.caption: Despite NAC, his INR keeps climbing and encephalopathy deepens: he is getting worse, not better.

steps.title: Day 2 bloods
steps.text: Daniel now meets **King's College Criteria** for paracetamol-induced liver failure.

steps.lead: Arterial pH below 7.3, and PT above 100 s with creatinine above 300 and grade III/IV encephalopathy: Daniel needs an **urgent liver transplant**.

steps.title: Acute liver failure: the pathway
nodes: Treat the cause: NAC for paracetamol
Treat encephalopathy: lactulose ± rifaximin; mannitol for cerebral oedema

steps.lead: Daniel has no cirrhosis, but if he had: **spironolactone plus furosemide** for ascites, and TIPS for refractory ascites or varices, at the cost of more encephalopathy.
Daniel's care follows **NICE** paracetamol overdose guidance, the **King's College Criteria** for transplant, and **NICE NG50** for anyone with cirrhosis.

steps.text: In a cirrhotic with ascites who becomes febrile or confused, think **spontaneous bacterial peritonitis**: tap the ascites and give **IV ceftriaxone** (or cefotaxime).
Do not give FFP just to 'correct' Daniel's INR unless he is bleeding. The INR is your best guide to liver function and transplant need.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why paracetamol kills hepatocytes (NAPQI, glutathione), why NAC works, why INR rises first (factor VII), or why ammonia causes asterixis.

steps.lead: Daniel's failing liver explains each result: low glucose (metabolic), high INR and low albumin (synthetic), jaundice (excretory).

steps.title: Paracetamol to liver failure
nodes: Glutathione stores depleted (worse with alcohol, starvation)
steps.caption: NAC replenishes glutathione, so NAPQI is neutralised again.

steps.lead: Daniel's heavy drinking and poor eating had already **depleted his glutathione**, so NAPQI built up quickly. NAC refills it.
Daniel's INR rose within a day because **factor VII** has the shortest half-life of the clotting factors.

steps.q: Why does Daniel have a flapping tremor?
o: Bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia
steps.r: The liver cannot clear **ammonia** through the urea cycle; ammonia disrupts **astrocytes** and neurotransmission.

steps.lead: Daniel's **ammonia** is not being converted to urea, so it reaches his brain and causes confusion and asterixis. Lactulose traps it in the gut.
**Budd-Chiari** is a different route: blocked hepatic vein outflow congests the sinusoids and starves hepatocytes of oxygen.
If Daniel had cirrhosis, an infection, GI bleed or **binge** could tip him into **acute-on-chronic** failure.

mcq.q: Which INR value defines coagulopathy in acute liver failure?
mcq.r: **INR >1.5** with encephalopathy defines acute liver failure.

mcq.q: Which sign is a cardinal feature of grade II/III hepatic encephalopathy?
What is the classic triad of Budd-Chiari syndrome?
mcq.r: **Abdominal pain, ascites and hepatomegaly**; fever-jaundice-pain is Charcot's (cholangitis).

mcq.q: What is the best marker of liver synthetic function?
What is first-line treatment of hepatic encephalopathy?
mcq.r: **Lactulose**; rifaximin is an add-on for prophylaxis.

mcq.q: What is the antidote for paracetamol-induced liver failure?
What is the first-line treatment of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
What is the main complication of TIPS?
mcq.r: Shunting blood past the liver raises ammonia: **encephalopathy**.

mcq.q: What is the toxic metabolite of paracetamol?

technique.stem: A 42 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her partner, who found an empty packet of 32 paracetamol tablets 3 days ago. She has vomiting and right upper quadrant pain and is now confused. She is jaundiced with a coarse flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: jaundice plus confusion. Decide whether the liver has failed.
Overdose 3 days ago = **hepatic phase**; confusion with **asterixis** = encephalopathy; jaundice.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cholangitis gives fever, rigors and an obstructive picture; no fever here.
Withdrawal causes tremor and agitation, not a flap with jaundice.
Abscess gives a swinging fever, not encephalopathy days after an overdose.
Wernicke's is ataxia, ophthalmoplegia and confusion, without jaundice or a flap.

steps.x: **B. Acute liver failure.** Rule: jaundice + encephalopathy (asterixis) = liver failure.

technique.stem: A 29 year old man has acute hepatitis B. Over 2 days he becomes drowsy and disorientated. His ALT is 3200 IU/L (10–50) and bilirubin 140 μmol/L (<17). The team wants to know whether he meets the definition of acute liver failure.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: It asks for the test that **defines** acute liver failure.
He already has encephalopathy; the missing defining feature is coagulopathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **INR** (above 1.5) defines the coagulopathy of acute liver failure.

elim: Albumin has a long half-life (about 20 days) and falls too slowly.
ALP reflects cholestasis, not synthetic failure.
Ammonia is not part of the definition and correlates poorly with grade.
Ultrasound looks for structure and vessels, not function.

steps.x: **C. INR.** Rule: INR >1.5 + encephalopathy = acute liver failure.

technique.stem: A 24 year old woman took 40 paracetamol tablets over 2 days. She has right upper quadrant pain and vomiting. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg. Her paracetamol level is 18 mg/L, ALT 1450 IU/L (10–50) and INR 2.1.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Plan for discharge as the level is low

steps.x: Initial management of paracetamol overdose with liver injury.
**Staggered** overdose: the nomogram cannot be used. Liver injury is already present.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Charcoal only helps within 1 hour of a single ingestion.
Lactulose treats encephalopathy, which she does not have.
A low level is meaningless in a staggered overdose with a high ALT and INR.
Transplant is decided by King's College Criteria after NAC; she does not meet them yet.

steps.x: **B. IV N-acetylcysteine.** Rule: staggered overdose or deranged LFTs = NAC regardless of level.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is admitted with confusion. He has a coarse flapping tremor. His serum ammonia is raised. He is started on lactulose.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his confusion?
o: Ammonia crossing the blood-brain barrier and disrupting astrocytes

steps.x: A mechanism question for hepatic encephalopathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The liver cannot clear **ammonia** via the urea cycle; ammonia crosses the BBB and disrupts astrocytes.

elim: Hyponatraemia can confuse but does not cause a flap or raised ammonia.
Bilirubin causes jaundice, not encephalopathy in adults.
Subdural is a mimic to exclude but does not explain raised ammonia and a flap.
Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke's, not asterixis.

steps.x: **A. Ammonia and astrocytes.** Lactulose works by trapping ammonia in the gut.

practice.stem: A 46 year old woman has had acute hepatitis B for 10 days. Today she is drowsy and disorientated in time. She is jaundiced with a tender, smooth liver edge. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. Asterixis is present.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Viral hepatitis with new encephalopathy and an INR above 1.5 in a previously normal liver is acute liver failure.

steps.x: Diagnosis: viral hepatitis that has become something worse.
Encephalopathy (asterixis) on top of hepatitis, INR raised: the liver has **failed**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No alcohol history and withdrawal does not cause a flap or INR 3.4.
The cause is hepatitis B, and AIH does not explain sudden encephalopathy.
Abscess gives a swinging fever and a focal lesion.
Wernicke's gives ataxia and ophthalmoplegia, not asterixis.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man is admitted 3 days after taking 50 paracetamol tablets. He is jaundiced and increasingly confused. His INR is 3.8 and ALT 7200 IU/L (10–50).
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Asterixis (hepatic flap) is a cardinal feature of grade II/III hepatic encephalopathy in acute liver failure.

steps.x: 'Most likely finding': which sign fits acute liver failure with confusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Caput medusae needs portal hypertension from chronic cirrhosis.
Dupuytren's is a chronic alcohol-related sign.
Kayser-Fleischer rings are Wilson's disease.
A palpable gallbladder suggests malignant biliary obstruction (Courvoisier).

steps.x: **A. Asterixis.** Acute failure lacks the chronic stigmata.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman, 3 weeks after giving birth, has 5 days of abdominal pain and swelling. She has tender hepatomegaly and shifting dullness. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. She takes no medicines and drinks no alcohol.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Abdominal pain, ascites and tender hepatomegaly in the peripartum period is the classic triad of Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis).

steps.x: Diagnosis: pain, ascites and a big liver in a prothrombotic state.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cholecystitis gives RUQ pain and fever, not ascites with a large liver.
Hepatitis A gives jaundice and high ALT but rarely ascites.
Portal vein thrombosis causes portal hypertension but not tender congestive hepatomegaly.
Pre-eclampsia needs hypertension and proteinuria; BP is normal.

steps.x: **B. Budd-Chiari syndrome.** Confirm with Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites has 2 days of diffuse abdominal pain and new confusion. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. Ascitic tap is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, abdominal pain and confusion in a cirrhotic with ascites, with ascitic neutrophils above 250 per mm³, is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a complication of chronic liver failure.
Cirrhotic + ascites + fever + confusion. Ascitic neutrophils over 250.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain to the back and high amylase; the tap would not be the clue.
HCC causes weight loss and a mass, not fever with ascitic neutrophilia.
Perforation causes sudden severe pain and peritonism, with polymicrobial fluid.
TB peritonitis is subacute, lymphocytic.

steps.x: **D. SBP.** Ascitic neutrophils >250/mm³ is the diagnostic cut-off.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman at 35 weeks of pregnancy has 1 week of epigastric pain and itch, followed by jaundice and vomiting. Her BP is 128/80 mmHg and pulse rate 100 bpm. She is mildly confused.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Third-trimester abdominal pain then jaundice with hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy and encephalopathy is acute fatty liver of pregnancy, a cause of acute liver failure.

steps.x: Diagnosis of liver failure in late pregnancy.
Third trimester; pain then jaundice; confusion. Labs: **hypoglycaemia** and high INR = liver failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Gallstones cause colic or obstructive jaundice, not failure with hypoglycaemia.
HELLP is hypertensive with low platelets; BP is normal and hypoglycaemia favours AFLP.
Hepatitis E needs travel or exposure and very high ALT.
Hyperemesis is first trimester vomiting without liver failure.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man has 2 weeks of jaundice, nausea and malaise after a heavy binge. He drinks 80 units of alcohol a week. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. He has tender hepatomegaly.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his liver dysfunction?
practice.e: Acute jaundice after a binge on chronic heavy drinking, with AST:ALT above 1.5 and neutrophilia, is alcoholic hepatitis.

steps.x: Cause question: look at the LFT ratio and the history.
Chronic heavy drinking + binge trigger + fever. Labs: **AST:ALT >1.5**, neutrophilia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cholangitis gives rigors, RUQ pain and an obstructive (ALP-dominant) picture.
Hepatitis C is usually silent and ALT-dominant.
Paracetamol toxicity gives ALT in the thousands.
PBC is cholestatic in middle-aged women.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man is found confused at home with jaundice. No history is available. He has asterixis and no stigmata of chronic liver disease. His ALT is 5600 IU/L (10–50) and INR 3.2. Viral serology is pending.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause?
practice.e: Paracetamol is the commonest cause of acute liver failure in the UK; a paracetamol level, alongside viral serology, identifies the cause.

steps.x: 'Identify the cause' of acute liver failure.

clues: no stigmata of chronic liver disease
steps.x: Acute liver failure, cause unknown; viral tests already sent.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: CT head may be needed for confusion but does not find the liver cause.
Biopsy is risky with INR 3.2 and rarely needed.
MRCP images the ducts; ALT in the thousands is not obstructive.
Ammonia supports encephalopathy but does not give the cause.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman with acute liver failure is being assessed. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. The team needs one blood test that best reflects how her liver synthetic function changes over the next few hours.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: INR is the best marker of synthetic function because factor VII has a short half-life, so it changes within hours.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: ALT reflects injury and can fall as the liver dies.
Albumin is synthetic but takes weeks to change.
Bilirubin reflects excretion, not synthesis.
GGT is a cholestasis and alcohol marker.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is admitted with confusion after constipation for 5 days. He has asterixis. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. There is no fever, bleeding or abdominal tenderness.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Oral lactulose is first-line for hepatic encephalopathy; rifaximin is added for prophylaxis against recurrence.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Mannitol is for cerebral oedema, mainly in acute liver failure.
Rifaximin is an add-on to reduce recurrence, not first alone.
Protein restriction is no longer advised; it worsens malnutrition.
TIPS would worsen encephalopathy.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman with paracetamol-induced acute liver failure has received N-acetylcysteine. Her pulse rate is 120 bpm and BP 88/50 mmHg despite fluids. She has grade IV encephalopathy.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue NAC and repeat bloods in 48 hours
Give vitamin K and discharge planning
practice.e: PT over 100 s, creatinine over 300 μmol/L and grade III/IV encephalopathy meet King's College Criteria: urgent liver transplant is the definitive treatment.

steps.x: 'Next step' after NAC: apply King's College Criteria.
PT >100 s + creatinine >300 + grade III/IV encephalopathy = King's criteria met.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Waiting 48 hours risks death; criteria are already met.
Vitamin K does not fix synthetic failure; she is critically ill.
Dialysis may be needed for renal support but does not treat the liver failure.
Rifaximin is encephalopathy prophylaxis in chronic disease.

practice.stem: A 59 year old woman with cirrhosis and ascites has abdominal pain and fever. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. Ascitic fluid neutrophil count is 520 per mm³.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is treated first with IV antibiotics such as ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or ciprofloxacin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Drainage alone leaves the infection untreated.
Spironolactone treats ascites, not infection.
Surgery is for secondary peritonitis (perforation), not SBP.
TIPS is for refractory ascites or varices.

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman took 60 paracetamol tablets 6 hours ago. She is started on N-acetylcysteine. She asks how the treatment protects her liver.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of N-acetylcysteine?
practice.e: Excess paracetamol forms NAPQI; once glutathione is depleted, NAPQI causes centrilobular necrosis. NAC replenishes glutathione.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: NAC does not block CYP450.
That is activated charcoal.
NAC does not change renal excretion.
NAC prevents injury; it does not regenerate hepatocytes.

prompts.q: What is liver failure and what are its main causes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: loss of synthetic, metabolic and detox function; name the big three causes.

points.p: Severe loss of synthetic, metabolic and detoxification function
points.why: Each lost function gives a test result.
Hepatitis B/C cause chronic; A, B, E can cause acute.
Commonest cause of acute liver failure in the UK.

prompts.q: What defines acute liver failure and how does it present?

points.p: Markedly raised transaminases, modest ALP/bilirubin rise

points.why: No chronic stigmata in pure acute failure.

prompts.q: Which features suggest chronic or decompensated liver failure, and which complication must you not miss?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: stigmata of cirrhosis and portal hypertension.

points.p: Background cirrhosis with gradual decline and portal hypertension
points.why: Acute-on-chronic if an insult tips it.
Fever, pain or confusion in a patient with ascites.

prompts.q: What are the classic presentations of paracetamol hepatotoxicity and alcoholic hepatitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: timing for paracetamol, ratio for alcohol.

points.p: Paracetamol hepatic phase: vomiting, RUQ pain, tender liver, asterixis
Alcoholic hepatitis: chronic drinking with binge trigger
Alcoholic hepatitis labs: AST:ALT >1.5, high bilirubin, neutrophilia

prompts.q: Name the rarer causes of liver failure and their clues.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pregnancy and prothrombotic states.

points.why: Increased risk in pregnancy; Doppler ultrasound.

prompts.q: Which investigations diagnose liver failure, assess severity and find the cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: INR defines; grade the encephalopathy; level and serology for the cause.

prompts.q: How do you manage acute liver failure in the first hours?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: treat the cause, support, treat the brain.

points.p: Treat the cause: N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol
points.why: Give in staggered overdoses regardless of level.
Early transfer to a liver unit.

points.p: Lactulose; rifaximin add-on; mannitol for cerebral oedema

prompts.q: What are the King's College Criteria for transplant in paracetamol liver failure?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one criterion alone, or three together.

points.p: OR PT >100 s AND creatinine >300 AND grade III/IV encephalopathy

prompts.q: How do you manage complications of chronic liver failure?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ascites, SBP, portal hypertension.

points.p: TIPS for refractory ascites or recurrent variceal bleeding

prompts.q: Why does paracetamol overdose damage the liver, and why does NAC work?
Why do encephalopathy and a high INR occur in liver failure?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ammonia and factor VII.

points.p: Liver cannot clear ammonia via the urea cycle
points.why: Lactulose traps ammonia in the gut.

points.p: Ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier and disrupts astrocytes
Reduced clotting factor synthesis, especially factor VII
points.why: Shortest half-life, so INR rises first.

glossary.INR: International normalised ratio; a clotting test showing how well the liver makes clotting factors.
glossary.PT: Prothrombin time, the clotting test from which the INR is calculated.
glossary.asterixis: A coarse flapping tremor of outstretched, dorsiflexed hands; sign of hepatic encephalopathy.
glossary.hepatic encephalopathy: Confusion and reduced consciousness caused by toxins the failing liver cannot clear.
glossary.acute-on-chronic: Sudden decompensation of an already cirrhotic liver after an acute insult.
glossary.decompensation: When a cirrhotic liver can no longer cope, causing jaundice, ascites, bleeding or encephalopathy.
glossary.cirrhosis: End-stage scarring of the liver with nodules and loss of function.
glossary.portal hypertension: Raised pressure in the portal vein, usually from cirrhosis, causing varices, ascites and splenomegaly.
glossary.ascites: Free fluid in the peritoneal cavity.
glossary.shifting dullness: Dullness to percussion that moves when the patient rolls; a sign of ascites.
glossary.spider naevi: Small red skin lesions with radiating vessels, seen in chronic liver disease.
glossary.gynaecomastia: Male breast enlargement, seen in chronic liver disease from raised oestrogen.
glossary.SBP: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: infection of ascitic fluid without a surgical cause.
glossary.Budd-Chiari syndrome: Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, usually thrombosis, causing pain, ascites and hepatomegaly.
glossary.Doppler ultrasonography: Ultrasound that shows blood flow in vessels.
glossary.acute fatty liver of pregnancy: Third-trimester fat infiltration of the liver causing acute liver failure.
glossary.haemochromatosis: Inherited iron overload that can cause cirrhosis.
glossary.NAC: N-acetylcysteine, the paracetamol antidote that replenishes glutathione.
glossary.N-acetylcysteine: The paracetamol antidote; it replenishes glutathione.
glossary.NAPQI: N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine, the toxic paracetamol metabolite.
glossary.glutathione: A liver antioxidant that neutralises NAPQI.
glossary.centrilobular: Around the central vein of the liver lobule (zone 3), where paracetamol damage is worst.
glossary.King's College Criteria: Criteria used to decide which patients with acute liver failure need urgent transplant.
glossary.lactulose: An osmotic laxative that traps ammonia in the gut; first-line for hepatic encephalopathy.
glossary.rifaximin: A poorly absorbed antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria.
glossary.mannitol: An osmotic diuretic used to reduce cerebral oedema.
glossary.cerebral oedema: Brain swelling, a major cause of death in acute liver failure.
glossary.ceftriaxone: A third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic, first line for SBP.
glossary.TIPS: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt: a stent linking portal and hepatic veins to lower portal pressure.
glossary.spironolactone: An aldosterone antagonist diuretic, the mainstay for ascites.
glossary.furosemide: A loop diuretic added to spironolactone for ascites.
glossary.ammonia: A toxic by-product of protein breakdown normally cleared by the liver's urea cycle.
glossary.urea cycle: Liver pathway that converts ammonia into urea for excretion.
glossary.astrocytes: Brain support cells that take up ammonia and swell when it accumulates.
glossary.factor VII: The clotting factor with the shortest half-life, so it falls first in liver failure.
glossary.ALT: Alanine aminotransferase, an enzyme released by damaged hepatocytes.
glossary.AST: Aspartate aminotransferase; AST higher than ALT suggests alcohol.
glossary.ALP: Alkaline phosphatase, raised mainly in cholestasis.
glossary.alcoholic hepatitis: Acute inflammation of the liver from heavy drinking, often after a binge.
glossary.staggered overdose: Overdose taken over more than an hour, so the treatment nomogram cannot be used.
glossary.FFP: Fresh frozen plasma, a blood product containing clotting factors.
